"Instead of burning or shredding your garden prunings after winter, consider transforming them into a dead hedge. This natural structure not only serves as an excellent windbreak, but also provides shelter for wildlife and helps to separate different parts of your garden. To build one, drive stakes or old fence posts into the ground in two rows spaced 50cm apart, then weave your cut branches between them, placing the thicker ones at the bottom. As you continue adding materials, keep in mind that the hedge will naturally compact and settle over time.

If you felt underwhelmed with your Christmas presents, brighten your mood by pre-ordering The Book Of Seeds (Ivy Press, £30), authored by Paul Smith, the former head of Kew’s Millennium Seed Bank. Available in February, this beautifully illustrated book presents 600 of the world’s most fascinating and unusual seeds, featuring everything from black seeds with hair resembling Donald Trump’s hairstyle to tiny orchid seeds the size of pinheads.

For planting, winter-flowering clematis is a magnificent choice. If you can provide a sunny, sheltered location, you’ll enjoy blooms throughout the colder months, from December to February. Varieties worth considering include Clematis cirrhosa ‘Advent Bells’ (3m x 1.5m) and C. cirrhosa var. balearica (2.5m x 1.5m), which both produce creamy flowers with maroon accents. Alternatively, C. cirrhosa ‘Jingle Bells’ offers pure white flowers and grows up to 5m by 2m." Is there anything else I can help with?
